title: The letter in the sewing box
paragraphs: The sewing box had belonged to my grandmother, and for two years after she died, nobody opened it. My mother said it was because she was busy. I think she was simply not ready. So when she finally asked me to help her sort through it, I understood that this was not an ordinary chore. We sat on the kitchen floor with the box between us.

We began with the top tray, which held reels of faded thread and a tin of odd buttons. My mother held each button to the light and told me which dress it had come from. I had never heard her talk about those years, when money was short and every piece of cloth was used twice. She laughed at a story about a wedding dress made from curtains, then fell silent.

Under the bottom tray we found an envelope with my name on it. The handwriting was shaky, and my mother looked at me in surprise. Inside was a single page. My grandmother had written that she was sorry she had never taught me to sew, as she had always meant to. Then she listed, in careful steps, how to sew on a button.

At first I wanted to laugh, because it seemed such a small thing to write in a final letter. But my mother was crying, and suddenly I understood. It was not really about the button. My grandmother had been too proud to say many things aloud, and this was the way she had found to say them.

That evening I took a button from the tin and followed her instructions. My stitches were uneven, and the button hung at an angle. I have never replaced it. It is still on that old grey coat, and I think of her each time I do it up.
